t: one who claims against his fellow movable property etc.. But if he claims land from him, he does not swear (see below 5:1).
and admitted part of it. The defendant admitted part of the claim to the claimant and denied the rest.

as it says, "of which he says, 'This is it'" etc.. The continuation of the verse: "the matter of both parties shall come before God," and the Sages interpreted this to mean that the defendant must swear before the court on his claim (see Mekhilta of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai 22:8). The phrase "of which he says, 'This is it'" the Sages interpreted to mean that the defendant says he has only "this," that is, that he admits part of the claim and not all of it (see Mekhilta of Rabbi Yishmael, Mesechta deNezikin, section 15).
from tradition. The Sages' tradition.

for any iniquity and any sin he does not stand, but he stands for an oath. The testimony of a single witness is not accepted and does not stand for the purpose of imposing punishment, but it can obligate an oath.
you have no one liable to an oath by Torah law except three. There are only three cases in which a person is liable to an oath by Torah law (see also Hilchot Shevuot 11:5).
in Hilchot Sechirut. 1:2.

but all who swear and take... all swear by the enactment of the Sages. In all the cases where the law is that the claimant swears and on the basis of the oath takes what he claims, the oath is a rabbinic enactment and not from the Torah.

hired worker. The Sages enacted that a hired worker who claims his wages from the employer swears that he did not receive payment and takes his wages, since the employer is busy with his workers and does not always remember whether he paid (Hilchot Sechirut 11:6).

and one who was wounded and one who was robbed. The Sages penalized the one who wounds and the one who robs, so that in certain cases the one who claims against them is trusted to swear and take from them, in order that damages and lawlessness among people not increase (see Hilchot Chovel 5:4, Hilchot Gezelah 4:1-2, Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevuot 7:3).

and one who impairs his document and the like. If the defendant claimed that the entire debt in the document was paid and the claimant admitted that part of it was paid, he collects the rest of the debt by oath (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 14:1-3, where other cases are mentioned in which the lender swears and takes).

and likewise all who swear on a claim of doubt. There are cases in which the Sages obligated the claimant to swear even though the claimant does not make a certain claim but only suspects the defendant.

such as partners and sharecroppers. A partner can make his partner swear that he did not take from the partnership's business in his hands more than what is due him, and likewise the field owner can make the sharecropper who tends the field for a share of the crop swear that he did not take more than what was agreed between them (and see Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 9:1, where other people who swear on a claim of doubt are detailed and where it is explained why they swear on a claim of doubt).

even though they are rabbinic, they are like a Torah oath with taking hold of an object. Even though these oaths were enacted by the Sages, he nevertheless swears holding a Torah scroll in his hand, as one swears the Torah oath (see Hilchot Shevuot 11:8).
one who claims movable property from his fellow. The claimant demands movable property from his fellow.

and gave it immediately, and said, "I have of yours only this, and here it is for you". When the defendant offered the claimant the movable property he admitted to, saying "here it is for you," there is now no claim except regarding the rest, and regarding the rest the defendant denies everything (see also below 3:15).
but you forgave me. What you had in my possession.
or you gave or sold. Or he claimed that he gave it to him as a gift or sold it to him.

or he claimed wheat from him and he admitted barley. He claimed one thing and the defendant admitted something else that he did not claim from him; even in this case they do not obligate the oath of one who admits part (see below 3:8-10).
in Hilchot Shevuot. 11:8-13.
they seize his property. The court takes from his property and gives it to the claimant.
I do not depart from the law of the Torah: either swear or pay me. I do not waive the Torah's law by which you are obligated to pay unless you swear.

and he may excommunicate anyone who claims against him something that is not so, and he pays. By enactment of the Geonim, in certain cases where a person suspects another of making a false claim against him and cannot obligate him to swear, he can impose a general ban (curse) on whoever lies against him in that matter, without mentioning the suspect's name, to threaten him not to claim against him improperly (see Maggid Mishneh, Hilchot Gezelah 4:7-8, Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 3:11).
an oath by rabbinic enactment. By enactment of the Sages.
to reverse the oath. To obligate the claimant to swear, in order to be exempt from swearing himself, so that the claimant swears and takes.
and if he does not want to swear, he goes. If the claimant does not want to swear, he leaves with nothing.
for if the claimant said, "I do not want this enactment that the Sages enacted for me". To swear while holding an object and take.
but I am like all other claimants. Like an ordinary person who claimed against his fellow, while the other denies everything.

and if he wanted to reverse it onto the claimant, they obligate the claimant to swear a heset oath and take, or he goes. If the defendant does not want to swear a heset oath, he can demand that the claimant swear in his place and take (for the heset oath can be reversed onto the claimant, as below, halachah 6). And if the claimant does not want to swear, he takes nothing.
from those who swear and are exempted. From those who swear by rabbinic enactment in order to be exempt from payment.
they excommunicate. They place him under ban, as with one who did not accept the law, who is banned (Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:14).
if he did not come and did not claim, his ban. If he did not come to court to settle the matter and have the ban lifted from him.
they give him lashes for rebelliousness. The judge strikes him with a whip "according to what seems proper to him in view of his stubbornness" (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevuot 6:1).

like anyone on whom a ban of thirty days has fallen, who is struck. There are cases in which they deal differently with one who does not seek to have his ban lifted, and the matter depends on the circumstances of the case (see Hilchot Talmud Torah 7:6-7 and Rabbi Y. Kafach there).
and they do not seize his property, since he is not obligated to an oath by Torah law. Only one obligated to an oath by Torah law must pay if he did not swear, as above, halachah 4.
if he wanted to reverse the oath onto the claimant. That instead of the defendant swearing and being exempt, the claimant swears and takes what he claims.
and you have no one who etc.. This is the only case in which a claimant swears a heset oath and takes.
and you have no oath that is reversed except the heset oath alone. Because it is a light oath, the Sages enhanced the defendant's power to reverse the oath onto the claimant (Maggid Mishneh).

but an oath of the Torah or of the Sages' oaths that is like one of the Torah is not reversed. And see below 2:4-7 that if the defendant is suspected of false swearing, the claimant is made to swear and takes.
a heset oath is imposed only on a claim of certainty. That the claimant makes a certain claim against the defendant.
my father told me. An orphan who claimed on the basis of what he heard from his father before he died.
he commanded me in the presence of witnesses that he has a maneh with you. My father said in front of witnesses that he is designating for me this money he has with you as part of his will.
you misled me in the accounting. And you gave me less than you should have given, or took from me more than you should have taken.
I certainly have a maneh in your possession. The claimant makes a certain claim that he has a maneh with the defendant.

he swears a heset oath that he does not know, and pays barley. Since he admits in principle that he owes him but does not know whether wheat or barley, he pays barley, whose value is less than wheat, since at the very least he owes him its value. And as for the difference between wheat and barley, on which he neither admits nor denies, he is liable to a heset oath like any defendant who makes a claim of perhaps (and see below 3:10 for the law where he denied the wheat claim and admitted that he owes barley).
because he knows with certainty that he is liable. It is clear to the defendant that he was liable, and he admitted it.
and this one claimed against him a claim of certainty. The claimant claims with certainty that his debt was not paid.

and he is unsure whether he was released or not released. The defendant is unsure whether he paid the debt or not, and since it is clear that the defendant was liable, he must now pay the claimant, and his claim that he does not know whether he returned it or not does not release him from his responsibility until he remembers with certainty what he did.
but if he has no claimant and he admitted on his own... he is not obligated to pay. For there is no claim of certainty here, only a person's doubt whether he is liable.

swear a heset oath and go; you swear a heset oath and take. The claimant demanded that the defendant swear if he wants to be exempt from his claim, and the defendant reversed the oath and demanded that the claimant swear and take what he claims.
and the claimant said, "I do not want to swear". And he wants to reverse the oath back onto the defendant, to swear and be exempt or to pay.

and he may excommunicate in general anyone who owes me and does not give me. If the claimant does not want to swear, he may impose a ban on one who does not give him what he owes him, to threaten the defendant to pay (see above, halachah 4, for the explanation).
he may excommunicate. He may impose a ban before the court.

and they not cause the name of Heaven to be uttered in vain, nor bring a false report. When a person swears by God's name on a false claim made against him, even though he swears truthfully, there is nonetheless an oath by God's name and an unnecessary mention of the name of Heaven (for the entire need for the oath arises here from a false claim), and this involves something of the prohibition "you shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain" (Exodus 20:7), which also includes a vain oath (see Hilchot Shevuot 12:9-11, and see also there 11:18 and Radvaz there).
the one who administers the oath may roll onto him whatever he wishes. The one administering the oath may add further claims, and the one swearing must swear on them as well within the original oath.

from matters that if he admitted them, he would be liable for money. The one administering the oath may roll in only claims for which the one swearing would have been liable to pay had he admitted them, but claims on which he would not be liable to pay in any case he may not add to the original oath (and see also Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 10:2).
and how far does the power of rolling extend. How far he may go in the additional claims he adds to the original claim.
and we have already explained. Hilchot Sechirut 11:9.
for one does not roll onto the hired worker. A hired worker who comes to swear in order to take his wages is treated leniently, and they do not roll onto him that he swear on additional claims.
and rolls onto it the other matters. He includes in the severe oath the claims for which a light oath is owed.
one does not administer a heset oath to him. Because even if he said he would give it to him, he is not obligated by speech alone without an act of acquisition.
"you cursed me," "you spread an evil name about me"... they do not ban over this. Since there is no obligation of payment for such acts.
you wounded me. The claimant claimed that the other wounded him, and the one who wounds is liable for five payments: damage, pain, medical costs, loss of time, and shame (Hilchot Chovel 1:1).

for although he does not pay a fine on his own admission etc.. If a person admitted in court to something that obligates him to a payment defined as a fine, he is exempt from paying it (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 2:8), and therefore one who denies a claim that would obligate him to a fine is exempt from swearing on it. As for the payments of one who wounds mentioned here, some of them are defined as a fine, which one who admits them is not obligated to pay, but the payments for loss of time and medical costs are not defined as a fine, and therefore if he admitted them he is liable; so too shame, although it is a fine, one who admits it is liable (see Hilchot Chovel 5:6-7).

you shamed me... if it was in a place where fines are collected, he swears a heset oath etc.. Although he pays shame on his own admission, nevertheless courts outside the Land of Israel that are not ordained do not judge cases of fines, including cases of shame (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 5:9-10).
he is liable to pay. Since he admitted that he was already obligated in court, it is like any debt.
anyone suspected regarding an oath. One suspected of swearing falsely.
even if the claimant wished. Even if the claimant is willing to accept his oath, they do not administer it to him.

whether he swore falsely an oath of utterance etc.. For each of the types of oaths on which he swore falsely, and likewise if he swore a vain oath, he becomes suspect (for the definition of the oaths mentioned here see Hilchot Shevuot 1:1-8).

and likewise anyone disqualified from testimony because of a transgression etc.. All those disqualified from testimony are also disqualified from swearing, whether disqualified by the Torah or by the Sages (for the laws of those disqualified from testimony because of transgression see Hilchot Edut, chapter 10).

a person does not become suspect until witnesses come against him that he committed a transgression for which he is disqualified etc.. Likewise regarding testimony, he is not disqualified unless witnesses testified that he committed a transgression (see Hilchot Edut 12:1-2).
and it is not proper to make him a witness at the outset. It is not proper to designate him as a witness for matters that must be done before witnesses.
they administer an oath to him etc.. Even though he admitted he committed a transgression, they administer an oath to him, since he is not believed to disqualify himself.
and not because you committed a transgression are you forbidden to swear truthfully. For even according to his words that he is disqualified, he is permitted to swear if he swears the truth.
an enactment of the Sages etc.. By enactment of the Sages, when a person is obligated to a Torah oath and is suspect and cannot swear, the claimant swears and takes.
and since he cannot swear, he pays. For one obligated to a Torah oath who did not swear must pay (see above 1:4).

the suspect was a bailee and claimed that the deposit was lost or stolen. And he is obligated by Torah law to swear the oath of bailees, that the object was lost from him in a way for which he is not responsible and that he did not lay a hand on it.

his opponent cannot swear and take, for he does not claim with certainty that he ate it. The oath of bailees is not based on a certain claim by the depositor, for he does not know what happened to the deposit (see also Hilchot Sechirut 2:7), and therefore he cannot swear in place of the bailee and take. Therefore in this case the bailee is exempt and does not pay (Maggid Mishneh).
Therefore, if the bailor claims etc.. Since he makes a definite claim, he swears and collects, as the Sages instituted.

If a suspect becomes liable to an oath by Rabbinic law etc.. When a suspect becomes liable to a Rabbinic oath, if it is a case where the claimant swears and collects, the suspect does not swear, and he also cannot collect without an oath; rather the defendant is exempted by a heset oath.
Likewise, one who impugns his own document, and anything similar. See above 1:2 in the commentary.

Or if the borrower claimed that he repaid it and said, "Let him swear to me". When a lender claims repayment from a borrower and brings a promissory note, and the borrower claims he repaid, he may demand that the lender swear to him that he was not repaid (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 14:2). If the lender is suspect regarding oaths, the defendant swears a heset oath and is exempt. Even though in this case, and in the cases of one who impugns his document and the like, the oath obligation is a stringency that the Sages imposed, and by Torah law the lender collects without an oath (since in all these cases he has a document that proves his claim), nevertheless if he is suspect regarding oaths and cannot swear, he cannot collect without an oath, and the defendant swears a heset oath and is exempt (contrary to the opinion of the Ra'avad here and the Ba'al HaMa'or at the end of Hilchot Shevuot - see Yad Peshutah).
If he was suspect among those who swear on a claim of doubt. For example, a partner (see above 1:5 in the commentary).

And his opponent does not swear, because this one was not liable to an oath by Torah law. For only where one is liable to a Torah oath did they institute that the claimant swears and collects (as above, halachah 4).

And because the claimant does not make a definite claim, so that he could swear on his claim. Moreover, even if he had been liable to a Torah oath, since he does not make a definite claim, he does not swear and collect (Lechem Mishneh).
For the heset oath itself is a rabbinic enactment. By strict law he would be exempt without an oath.

The defendant cannot turn the oath back on him. Even though a heset oath can generally be turned back, so that the defendant may demand that, instead of his swearing and being exempt, the claimant swear and collect what he claims (above 1:6).

We do not listen to this one to make it depend on something impossible. We do not listen to a defendant who wants to make the matter depend on the claimant and be exempt, since it is impossible to have him swear.
It is as if he turned the oath back on a minor. A minor does not swear (as below 5:10), so an oath cannot be turned back on him.
And his opponent may take back from him what he took. If the suspect swore and took, he must return what he took.

Or the one opposite him may swear and collect from him. If he swore a Torah oath and was exempted, the other may swear and collect from him (but a defendant who was liable through a claim of doubt or a heset oath is exempt if he is suspect, as above, halachot 6-7).
Always, a suspect is judged in this way. The law of a suspect remains in force without time limit.

Until he is flogged in court, if there were witnesses through whom he is flogged. He does not return to eligibility until he is flogged for the very transgression for which he was disqualified from testifying, if it is a transgression punishable by flogging and there were witnesses who warned him and made him liable to flogging.

And repents. If he was disqualified from testimony because of monetary transgressions that carry no flogging, he returns to eligibility only after it is evident from his deeds that he has fully repented (based on the Lechem Mishneh; see Hilchot Edut 12:3-10 and Kesef Mishneh there, halachah 4, who explained it differently).
And he returns to eligibility both for testimony and for an oath. Through these acts he regains eligibility to testify or to swear.
And he was established as suspect regarding oaths. He became suspect regarding oaths, so that he is not made to swear.
And we have already explained in Shevuot. Hilchot Shevuot 1:9, 11:20.
He must add a fifth. He returns the money he swore falsely about and adds a quarter of its value to the principal, so that together with the principal the addition is a fifth of the total.

He claimed that he owes him a debt, with witnesses and a kinyan. The claimant claimed he has witnesses that the defendant owes him money, and that the defendant even made a kinyan (act of acquisition) before them on this obligation (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 11:1).

Or he produced a document and it was validated. That on the basis of the obligation made before witnesses with a kinyan, a promissory note was written for the lender (see there), the document was validated in court, and the lender wants to collect his debt from the borrower by means of the document.
He must pay. For a borrower by document or kinyan is not believed to claim he repaid unless he brings witnesses to that effect (there).

And he is not suspect, for they did not testify that he did not repay etc.. Even though he pays, he does not become suspect regarding oaths, because the witnesses did not testify that he did not repay the debt, but only that the defendant borrowed from the claimant, and the defendant did not deny the loan itself but claimed that he now owes him nothing.

Until he admits to a perutah etc.. That he admits that he owes at least a perutah or something worth a perutah, and denies two ma'ah or something worth two ma'ah, so that the claim must be worth at least two ma'ah and a perutah.
A barley grain. A single grain of barley.
And how much are two ma'ah? The weight of thirty-two barley grains. For each ma'ah weighs sixteen barley grains (for the detailed calculation see Hilchot Shekalim 1:3).

Every "silver" mentioned in the Torah is the holy shekel, which is twenty ma'ah. Wherever the Torah mentions an amount of silver, it means the holy shekel mentioned in the commandment of the half-shekel (Exodus 30:13), where it says its weight is twenty gerah, and the Sages explained that this gerah is a ma'ah.

And all silver of their (the Sages') words etc.. Sums of silver set by the Sages were in the coins of Jerusalem in the Second Temple period. The coin called a "sela" that was in Jerusalem (whose weight equalled that of the holy shekel - see Hilchot Shekalim 1:2) was made of an alloy of one eighth silver and seven parts copper.
As we have explained. Hilchot Ishut 10:8, Hilchot Chovel UMazik 3:8.

And because the required denial of the claim, two silver, is of their (the Sages') words etc.. The Torah uses the word "silver" regarding the obligation of the oath of one who partially admits (Exodus 22:6), but does not specify an amount of silver. The Sages set the amount according to the pure silver coins in use in their time.

And my teachers ruled that the denial of the claim is the weight of nineteen and a half barley grains of silver. This is the view of Rabbi Yosef Migash (in his novellae to Shevuot 40a), who explained that the "two silver" mentioned by the Sages as the measure of a denial requiring an oath are two silver dinars of Jerusalem coinage; in addition he has another view regarding the weight of a dinar (see Yad Peshutah).
I have two ma'ah and a perutah of yours in my hand. This is the smallest amount that can bring one to the oath of partial admission, as above, halachah 1.
I owe you only a perutah - he is liable. For he admits to a perutah and denies two ma'ah.
As if he had admitted to nothing. He is not considered a partial admitter.
In what case does this apply?. That to be liable to the oath of partial admission, an admission of a perutah and denial of two ma'ah is required.
All vessels are like silver. Vessels are mentioned separately in the Torah and are not derived from "silver" as merchandise and produce are, so they need no particular minimum amount.

For anywhere that two witnesses would make him liable for a given sum of money, one witness makes him liable to an oath. As above 1:1. Just as two witnesses obligate payment through testimony involving at least a perutah, so too one witness obligates an oath.

For all who swear on a claim of doubt etc.. Partners and the like, who are liable to an oath on a claim of doubt, are liable only if the one making them swear suspects them regarding an amount of at least two silver ma'ah (Hilchot Shluchin VeShutafin 9:1-2).
A letech. Half a kor.

For the kind that he claimed he did not admit to, and the kind that he admitted to he did not claim. Even though in monetary terms he admitted part of the claim (barley is worth less than wheat), since he did not admit to part of what the claimant demanded but denied his whole claim and admitted something else that he did not claim, he is exempt from the oath of partial admission.
An actual item. An item with a description and form, not merely monetary value.
I deposited a ma'ah of silver with you. Coins of the ma'ah type (Lechem Mishneh, since a claim of one ma'ah is not enough for the oath of partial admission).
"You have a large menorah of mine" - "I have only a small menorah of yours" - he is exempt. Since these are two different menorahs and he did not admit to what was claimed from him.
Ritlin. A unit of weight.

Because he can scrape it and reduce it to five. Since he can scrape the menorah and reduce its thickness so that it weighs five, it is as if he admitted to part of the menorah that was claimed from him.
Belt. A girdle, made so that it cannot be cut and reduced.
But if he claimed a curtain... he swears, because it can be cut and reduced to ten. And so he has admitted to part of what was claimed from him.
He is exempt even from the value of the barley. When he admits to something not of the kind claimed, not only does he not swear, but he is also exempt from paying what he admitted.

And if the claimant seized the value of the barley, it is not taken from his hand. For when the injured party went and seized it, it showed that he had not been precise earlier, and now he retracts his admission and agrees with the one who caused the damage that his claim is correct (Rabbenu Chananel, Bava Kamma 35b; Yad Peshutah).
The admission is of the kind claimed, and he swears. Both the denial and the admission need not be of the same kind.
And before he completed his words and said "and a kor of barley," the defendant said to him, "I have only a kor of barley of yours". And the claimant says he had intended to claim barley as well.

If it appears to the judges that the defendant acted cunningly, he must pay. The barley; and he must also swear the oath of partial admission regarding the wheat (the accurate text of the Rambam according to Rabbi Yosef Shilat, and so it is explicit in the printed version and some manuscripts: "he is liable to an oath").
And if it was in his innocence, he is exempt. His law is as stated above, halachah 10.
And a kor of barley. After the defendant admitted to the wheat, the claimant continued and claimed barley from him as well.
For he claimed oil from him and he admitted to potsherds. For the wording of his claim shows he claimed only oil, and the other admitted to empty jars.
He is liable to an oath, since he claimed the jars and the oil, and he admitted to the jars. For the wording of his claim shows he claimed oil and jars, and the other admitted to the jars.
A maneh. One hundred dinars.

What difference does it make whether he became liable to him through a loan, a deposit, or damage?. Since in the end he admits to part of the debt claimed from him, it makes no difference for what reason he admits that he owes.
"I owe you only the vessel, and here, take it" - he is exempt. As above 1:3.
He includes in his oath that this is his vessel. When the defendant swears a heset oath on the rest of the claim, he includes in the oath that this is the vessel the claimant deposited with him.
He is liable to an oath. The oath of partial admission, since he admitted that he owes a vessel.
In this matter. The laws of partial admission.
And he is liable to a heset oath, as we have explained several times. One who denies everything must swear a heset oath (above 1:4 and elsewhere).
Something measured, weighed, or counted. That has a defined measure, weight, or quantity.
And he admits to him something measured, weighed, or counted. That the amount he admits will be defined by the same means of measure as the claim (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevuot 6:6).
I do not know how much it is. I do not know how many kor you gave me.
He is exempt. Since both the claim and the admission must be of a defined measure.
A projection. A protrusion jutting out from the wall.
And the other says "up to the window" - he is liable. Since both specified a defined measure.
Until he admits to something that he could have denied. That he admitted to something which, had he denied it, he would have been exempt.
I owe you only the fifty in the document. And he denied the fifty for which there is no document.
For his denial does not help against the document. And he is obligated to pay even if he denies it.
A document in which selaim are written without mentioning a number. A loan document stating that he lent him selaim, but not specifying how many.
The five selaim I have of yours are the ones written in it. What is written in the document refers to the five selaim that you owe me.

He is exempt, because he is like one returning a lost item. Since the document does not state how many selaim the loan was, the borrower cannot be held liable for more than two selaim (the minimum of the plural), so his admission to a third sela is an admission to part of the claimant's claim and would require an oath. But the Sages instituted that he does not swear, because the borrower could have claimed that he owes only two selaim and relied on the document being worded vaguely without specifying a number; so when he admits to a third sela, he is like one returning a lost item to the lender, giving him more than he could have received through the document. (But an ordinary partial admitter is not considered one returning a lost item, even though he could deny everything and be exempt with a heset oath, because the reason he does not deny everything is that he is uncomfortable lying and brazenly facing the creditor, and therefore his admission is not the return of a lost item - see Bavli Gittin 51b.)
And it is an enactment of the Sages that anyone who returns a lost item does not swear, as we have explained in its place. Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 13:20.
My father commanded that he has a maneh in your hands. My father stated in his will that he has a maneh (a hundred zuz) with you.
This one is returning a lost item. Since the son's claim is not definite, and if the defendant had wanted to lie he would not have hesitated to deny the whole claim.
And he is exempt even from the heset oath. Since the son's claim is a claim of "perhaps," as above 1:7.
And needless to say, if he admitted on his own etc.. Since the son did not claim from him at all.
But an heir who claimed and said etc.. The son of the lender who claimed on his own against the borrower or against the borrower's heir.
He is a partial admitter and swears. For the son's claim is a definite claim and is treated like any claim (and see below 5:9 regarding the law when the heir is a minor).
"I have a maneh of yours with this pledge". A lender who claims a debt and holds a pledge of the borrower.
"I owe you on it only fifty". The borrower claims that the loan for which the pledge was given was only fifty.
He is a partial admitter. And he is liable to an oath.
He swears. That he owes only fifty.
If the pledge was worth a hundred or more etc.. Since the lender holds the pledge, he may collect his debt from it after swearing how much the borrower owes him (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 13:3).

The lender swears that he is owed no less than eighty. He swears in the negative form that the borrower owes him no less than eighty, but he does not swear that the borrower owes him eighty, for in that case he would be lying in his oath, since he claims a hundred (see below 9:8).
He denied everything etc.. The defendant claimed that he owes nothing, and the item in the claimant's hand is a deposit he left with him.

He swears a heset oath on the twenty. The borrower who denied the entire claim swears a heset oath on the twenty, and the lender takes the eighty from the pledge after swearing about them, as stated at the beginning of the paragraph. [Note: In some manuscripts (and similarly in the printed editions) there is an addition here and the text reads: "The lender swears that he is owed no less than eighty and the borrower swears a heset oath on the twenty," and the meaning is the same as explained here.]
For he does not know. Whether he owes him those fifty.
Therefore he pays the maneh without an oath. Since he is obligated to swear a Torah oath and cannot, he must pay (as above 2:4).
And he may place him under a ban. The defendant may impose a ban, as above 1:11.

One who swears because of a single witness's testimony does not swear until he contradicts the witness, denies his testimony, and swears to his denial. An oath exempts him only if the defendant in his oath contradicts the witness's very words, and not if he denies only the conclusion that follows from the witness's words.
A document with one witness etc.. A document signed by only one witness, and the borrower claims he repaid the debt (see also Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 14:10).

And likewise a denier etc.. Who at first claimed he received nothing from the claimant, the claimant brought one witness that he lent to him or deposited with him, and the defendant retracted his first claim and claimed that he repaid or returned the deposit.

He is liable to an oath but cannot swear, and pays. In both these cases, had two witnesses testified to the loan in the document or to his denial, they would have obligated the defendant to pay money (see there 11:1, below 6:3), so one witness obligates an oath. Since the testimony is about the loan itself and the defendant does not contradict the witness but makes a different claim, he cannot swear and must pay (see also there, halachah 11).
A piece of silver. An ingot of silver.
He is liable to an oath but cannot swear. But had he contradicted the witness and claimed he had not seized at all, he would swear against him and be exempt (see also Hilchot Gezelah 4:14).
As will be explained. Below 6:1.
For anywhere that two witnesses would make him liable for a given sum of money, one makes him liable to an oath. As above 1:1.
As we have explained. Above, halachah 8.

That the admission of his mouth should not be greater than the testimony of witnesses. It should not turn out that an admission is more serious than testimony; therefore, just as one who partially admits with his mouth is liable to an oath on the rest that he denies, so too one found liable through witnesses swears on the rest.
As it is said etc.. The verse lists things on which one swears, and the Sages expounded that these exclude things not similar to them from an oath.
"To his fellow" - excluding Hekdesh. Hekdesh property, which is the property of the Most High and is not included in "his fellow."
Silver or vessels. Which are movable property.
And slaves, which are compared to land. They are equated to land in halachic terms (see Hilchot Genevah 2:2).
If there was a definite claim there. As above 1:7.
The Sages instituted that he swears on them like a Torah oath. An oath while holding a sacred object.
So that they would not treat Hekdesh property lightly. For if they did not swear a Torah oath regarding them, people would think that Hekdesh money is less serious than ordinary money.
Trenches. Narrow, long excavations.
On all of these he swears a heset oath. Since there is no admission and denial regarding movable property.
Since he is liable to an oath on part of the vessels that he denied. Since there is admission and denial regarding vessels.
He swears even about the land that he claimed along with them, for it is all one claim. And through the oath on movable property, an oath on the land is also attached.
It is like movable property regarding denial and admission. But for other matters it is considered land (see Hilchot Sechirut 2:4 and the commentary there).
Two silver. As above 3:1.
For the claim is not about the land itself but about the rent, which is movable property. And it is not a land claim, regarding which one is exempt from swearing.
I handed you a document. He handed his fellow a promissory note as a deposit.
And I had proof in it of ten dinars. That it states that the borrower owes ten dinars.
He turned it back on him. If the defendant turned the oath back on the claimant, so that he swears in his place and collects (as above 1:6).

He swears a heset oath that he had proof for ten dinars and they were lost with the loss of the document. The claimant swears about the amount in the document and that, because it is not in his hand, he cannot collect his debt.
He is exempt even from the heset oath. And all the more from a Torah oath, since one does not swear regarding documents.

He is exempt even from the heset oath, for even if he was negligent with it and it was lost, he is exempt. For the law is that guardians are not liable for the loss of documents (Hilchot Sechirut 2:1; and although it is explained there, halachah 3, that in a case of negligence they are liable for them, that refers to negligence of a kind considered as damaging directly, but if it was lost through negligence he is not liable - Responsa of the Bach 66).

As we have explained in Hilchot Chovel. See Hilchot Chovel UMazik 7:9; it seems the reference is to what is explained there, that one who burns his fellow's documents must pay the debt in the document, provided that the one who caused the damage admits to the sum written in the document and that this sum was lost because of the burning of the document. Likewise here, the oath is turned back on the claimant and he must swear about the sum in the document and that this sum was lost with the loss of the document (see Responsa of the Bach there and the Rambam LaAm, who explained the meaning of the reference in other ways; and see Maggid Mishneh, who explained this entire halachah differently).

One who says to his fellow, "The document that I have in your hands, I have a right in it" etc.. That one claimed that, according to the document they made between them which is in the defendant's hand, he has a monetary right (see Teshuvot HaGeonim, Harkavy, no. 496).
He claimed that the document was lost. The defendant.

We place a general ban for him. The claimant may impose a ban in general terms on whoever is hiding the document and claiming it was lost (see above 1:11 in the commentary). He cannot make him swear, since he does not claim against him definitely (see also Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 23:16).

For this part that he admitted to the minor is only like returning a lost item. For a minor (as also a deaf-mute or an imbecile) has no capacity to make a full claim and the defendant could deny it, and when he admits to part of the claim he is like one returning a lost item to him, and the Sages instituted that one does not swear the oath of partial admission where one is returning a lost item (see above 4:5).
For this is a single witness and there is no claimant. And a single witness does not obligate an oath without a claimant's claim.

Because he does not swear on account of a claim. The oath of bailees does not stem from a definite claim by the claimant but from doubt, and therefore this oath is sworn to a minor (see also Hilchot Sechirut 2:7).

A partner of the minor or a guardian over him. The Sages instituted that partners and guardians swear on a claim of doubt, so they swear to a minor. [Note: The vocalization of the word "apotropos" follows the Greek original. In the Rambam's autograph Commentary on the Mishnah this word is vocalized in several forms: sometimes the first pe has a kubutz, sometimes a patach (and in some places the pe has no vowel).]
Whether the minor comes on his own claim or on his father's claim. Whether the minor claims that the defendant owes him, or claims by virtue of the defendant having owed his father.

My teachers ruled that one does not swear a Torah oath on a minor's claim, but does swear a heset oath. Although one does not impose the oath of partial admission and the single-witness oath on a minor's claim, nevertheless his claim obligates a heset oath.

Even if he was a minor not sharp in business dealings. Even though for such a minor his sales and purchases have no validity (see Hilchot Mechirah 29:6), nevertheless a heset oath is sworn on his claim.
And he cannot turn it back on the minor. Even though a heset oath can generally be turned back on the claimant (as above 1:6).
And he does not even accept a general ban. His opponent cannot impose even a general ban on one who takes from him what is his.
The penalty of the oath. See Hilchot Shevuot 12:1-2.

If he claimed something from which the minor derives benefit, such as business dealings etc.. Although a minor's acts have no halachic validity, the Sages instituted that he may buy and sell movable goods in order to be able to support himself. Therefore, if he admitted things relating to these matters, he is bound by his admission.
Such as damages and injuries... he is exempt even after he comes of age. Since a minor is not liable (see Hilchot Chovel UMazik 4:20).
That a laborer may be hired for him. That he can find a hired worker who will agree to work for him.

A storekeeper who swore on his ledger. If a householder asked a storekeeper to give workers provisions as their wages and he would repay him later, and the storekeeper claimed against the employer that he gave them, while the workers claimed they took nothing from the storekeeper, both swear and collect and the householder loses (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 16:5).

For the minor has no benefit in this, since he must pay his workers etc.. Although the minor may have some benefit in the storekeeper paying the workers, he can pay them their wages himself, and if the workers have a need they can swear and collect from him. Therefore this is not considered a benefit for which the Sages instituted that one may swear and collect from a minor.
The deaf-mute. One who neither hears nor speaks (see Hilchot Ishut 2:26).
We do not attend to any claim of theirs. Since they have no understanding.
For a light oath... a severe oath. Between an oath without holding a sacred object and one with holding a sacred object (see above 1:2-3).
That I have with him for my wages. That he must pay me as salary.
Acceptable. Accepted.
And imagine in his mind that he is released from the debt. But by law he is not necessarily released by this.

For we judge by "since he could have said" in every place. It is a rule that when a defendant could make a good claim by which he would be exempt from the monetary claim, and he makes a lesser claim, he is exempt from the claim since he could have made the good claim ("migo"). Therefore we tell a sage that even if he is afraid to detail his claim because he knows it is not enough to be exempt, the court will argue the "migo" claim for him and exempt him, and so he has nothing to fear.
Or if he said to him, "I will give you a gift," and the like. And he is not bound by a promise without a kinyan (see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 3:1).
We do not accept it from him. We do not accept his words.
Rather he was established as a denier. The defendant is established as a liar, since it became clear through the witnesses that he lied, and he is not believed to claim he repaid.

But if he answered, "I owe you nothing" etc.. If at first he did not claim that he did not borrow but made claims implying that he owes him nothing, he does not become a denier through the witnesses, since he did not say that he was never obligated to him but only that he does not owe him now.
That he counted out money for him. That he counted money for him as he was giving it.
And they did not know what it was. For what purpose he gave it to him.
And he swears a heset oath. On the claimant's claim, as in any claim and denial where he denies everything and no witness testifies against him.

For anyone who says "I did not borrow," and witnesses came that he borrowed, is like one who says "I did not repay". Since it is known from the witnesses that he borrowed, and from the borrower's claim it emerges that he never repaid him, he is treated as one who borrowed and admits that he did not repay.
And the admission of a litigant is like a hundred witnesses. His admission that he did not repay obligates him even against the witnesses.

And the lender is not liable to an oath at all, since this one was established as a denier. Even if the borrower later claims after paying that he borrowed and repaid twice, and wants to make the lender swear that he did not originally receive repayment of his debt (as one can claim in an ordinary loan - see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 14:2), he cannot obligate him to an oath because he was established as a liar.
For the witnesses remember only a matter in which they are witnesses. It is possible that these people did see the loan but did not intend to testify to it, and therefore do not remember it.
"Give me the maneh that I lent you, when you were beside such-and-such pillar". That I lent you when you were beside a certain pillar.
Let him swear a heset oath that he repaid him. And he is exempt, even though he did not bring the witnesses.
For one who lends to his fellow before witnesses need not be repaid before witnesses. Therefore he can claim he repaid even if he brought no witnesses to that.
As we have explained. Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 11:1.
And he brought witnesses. Who saw that he admitted to him.
Even if he said, "There never was such a matter". I did not admit to you.

For he did not say to them, "You are my witnesses". Therefore it is possible he did not intend a binding admission (as below, halachah 7), and also it is possible he forgot the very fact that he admitted to him (as above, halachah 4).
Do you want so-and-so and so-and-so to testify?. Do you agree that so-and-so and so-and-so be witnesses to your admission?
Lest you press me in court tomorrow and I have nothing to give you. Lest you sue me in court and I be compelled to pay, and I have nothing with which to pay you.
For there is no testimony here. Such an admission is not considered an admission before witnesses.
Or the lender says in front of the borrower. That the people present are witnesses to the matter.

And the borrower is silent. And his silence shows his agreement (the rule here applies when he said the words in conversation, but if he said them as an admission, he need not say "you are my witnesses" - below 7:1, Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 3:6).
But with such testimony. Where the borrower did not accept the witnesses as witnesses to an admission.
"A kav of reshu," meaning that he has many debts. A "kav" is a measure of volume, and "reshu" means debts.
He said, "Whom do I owe except so-and-so?". He said before witnesses, "I owe no one, only so-and-so."
He said, "If I had money, would I not pay so-and-so and so-and-so?". And it is implied from his words that he owes them.

For a person is liable to show himself as not wealthy etc.. It is possible that he admitted that he owes them even though in truth he has no debt toward them, and did so in order that they would think him of limited means who owes money to others.
I did not intend to make myself appear sated. Not to appear as a rich and sated person.
As we have explained. Above, halachah 7.

Even though he did not say to them, "You are my witnesses". But if he spoke in conversation, it is not an admission unless he said "you are my witnesses" or "be witnesses against me" and the like (see above 6:7, Hilchot Edut 17:4, Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 3:6).
I admitted so as not to make myself appear sated. In order not to look like a rich and sated person.
He cannot claim and say, "I admitted in order to show that I am not rich". For he should have been concerned that he would be sued.
He claimed that he gave. That he repaid him after the admission.
And needless to say, if he admitted before three. For this is the law of an admission in court.
But they do not write. A document, on the basis of this testimony.

And they must consult him. It is not enough that the borrower told them to write and give; rather they must ask his permission after the document is signed, and only then may they hand it to the lender (since in a loan by document the lender has greater power, as the borrower cannot claim he repaid except with witnesses).
As we have explained. Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 11:1.
As will be explained. Below, halachah 3.

So that the two of them will not scheme to obligate another person. That one will admit to his fellow and instead of stating his name will tell the court the name of another person, so that they write a document in that other person's name and give it to the one to whom he admitted.
And he received. He claimed that his fellow owes him and asked that he be summoned to judgment.
They write and give to his opponent. For an admission in court is like a loan written in a document, and as below, halachah 5.

But if they were not a fixed court and did not send for him etc.. In this case the court does not have the formal status of a fixed court, and an admission before such a court is not considered a loan written in a document.
Even if he gathered them. The same one who came to admit.
And afterward the claimant came. After the admitter had left there.

Lest he give to him and this one be found claiming from him by the document. Since the admitter does not know that the document was given to his opponent, there is a concern that he will repay the debt and not take the document from him, and the other will claim from him again on the strength of the document.
Even though they did not take a kinyan from him. That they did not make a kinyan sudar to strengthen the matter (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:5 and the commentary there).
For here there is no concern lest he give to him and he be found claiming from him a second time. For he claimed a specific piece of land from him and one can see whether he gave it to him or not.
A document of admission that went out. That the admitter is sued to pay it by the holder of the document.

We suspect that perhaps there were two etc.. We suspect that he perhaps admitted before two, and they thought that the law of admission before them is like the law of admission in court, where they write and give a document even without being told to write, sign, and give.
We have already explained... as we have explained. Above, halachah 3.
That came to court. On their own.

Whether the judges said to him "You are obligated to give him". This is wording of a principled determination and not an absolute ruling, and nonetheless he may have paid on the basis of this instruction and not waited for the final decision.
Or whether they said to him "Give him". This is wording of a final decision and an instruction to carry out the ruling (see also below, halachah 6, Hilchot Genevah 2:15).
And went out and said, "I paid". After they left the court, the admitter claimed that he had paid the debt.

He is believed and swears a heset oath that he paid him. Since this admission does not have the status of a loan by document but of an oral loan, he need not repay in front of witnesses and is believed to claim that he paid him.
"Go and give him"... "You are obligated to give him". See above, halachah 4 in the commentary.
He was established as a denier regarding that money. Since he was contradicted by two witnesses, as above 6:1.
For this one slips away from them until they investigate his case. The defendant evades paying and carrying out the court's decision, and waits until they finish investigating his case.
He swears a heset oath that he paid him and is exempt. Since he was not established as a denier, he is believed with his oath.
Those expert in understanding. Those expert in knowing the laws.
They would say to him in front of the court. Those expert in understanding would say to the defendant in front of the court.
Be witnesses for me that he should not repay me, or that he should not swear to me, except before witnesses. Then he must repay him or swear to him before witnesses (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 15:1).
And here are witnesses. Who testify that he paid.
For he did not contradict his witnesses. At the beginning of his words, when he admitted that he owes.
And he is not like one who says "I never borrowed". For if he later brought witnesses that he paid, he would be required to pay, as above 6:3.
And even though he did not give a reason for the first claim. Even if he did not justify and explain why he made the first claim, he may make a different claim in its place.
To attach it to another claim. To shift and change his claim to another argument.

Unless he gave a reason for the claim he relied on, and it is implied, as he attached it, to this other claim. The defendant may return and make a new claim if he explains and clarifies the meaning of the first claim in a way that fits the claim he finally made (see examples below 10:8, 15:6).
All movable property is in the presumption of the one who has it in his possession. For the law of land see below, chapter 11 onward.
In his possession. In his domain.
Known to him. Known to be his.
He can claim up to the value. He can claim that he owes him up to the value of the pledge.
As we have explained. Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 13:3.
But things made for lending and renting. Items intended for rental and lending (below, halachah 9).
He rented it to him. He leased it to him.
They are in the presumption of their owners. By default he deposited or rented them to the defendant and did not sell them to him, and no testimony is needed for this.
And even if Shimon died, Reuven takes his vessels. For even their father had no way to hold the item, so there is no obstacle to taking it from the heirs.

And the Geonim ruled that he swears a heset oath, because we make claims for an heir. Although the heirs cannot claim with certainty that their father bought the vessel, the judges or the guardian make for them the claims their father could have made, and obligate the claimant to swear that the vessels are his (and see below 9:5 that in the Rambam's view he is not liable to an oath unless the heir made a definite claim against him).
Since he could say etc.. The holder is believed in his present claim since he could have denied and claimed that the vessel is not with him and thereby be fully exempt ("migo").
I do not know. I do not know in what way it left your hand, but it came to me from other people.
For he has no claimant. Since the claimant makes no specific claim against the defendant, but only claims that the item is his, the item is left in the holder's hand, and he is not made to swear.
It went out to the first owners that their vessels were stolen. If it became publicized that the claimant's vessels were stolen, and the holder claims he bought the item from another person.
This one swears while holding a sacred object how much he paid, and collects. The holder swears how much he paid for the item and collects the sum from the original owners.
As we have explained in Hilchot Genevah. 5:10-11.

He claimed, "You sold it to me or gave it to me," even though it was publicized as stolen... he swears a heset oath. Since the defendant denies that the item was stolen and claims he bought or received it from the owner.

From here you learn etc.. At the beginning of the previous paragraph it said that when the holder claims he bought the item from another and demands from the owners the money he paid for it, he must swear while holding a sacred object how much he paid. In this case a heset oath is not enough, although he could have claimed that the claimant sold it to him and then been exempt with a heset oath. From this it follows that in every case where one is liable to an oath while holding a sacred object, he cannot be exempted with a heset oath even if he could have made a claim that would have required only a heset oath (Kesef Mishneh; see Lechem Mishneh).
He swears while holding a sacred object. The defendant, and the claimant pays him its value (for examples of applying this rule see below 9:2, 10:3).

One who had in his hand things made for lending and renting etc.. The case here is where the claimant claims that the items belong to him and came into the defendant's hands unlawfully (based on Maggid Mishneh; see Lechem Mishneh, who discusses what novelty this halachah has relative to the above, halachah 5).
He admitted. The defendant.

This one claimed against him and said, "I rented them to you or lent them to you" - they are taken from his hand. For these vessels are in the presumption of the original owners, as above, halachah 3.
Pots. Cooking pots.
A copper ornament plated with gold. A copper ornament covered with gold.
But to lend them to others in order to benefit in return. To lend for free and receive some other benefit as indirect compensation.
Even if witnesses came that this one lent it or rented it. Several times.
They do not negate his presumption through them. The fact that he lent the item several times does not negate his presumption that it is not an item made for lending and renting.

Proof for our words. That even something not originally made for lending and renting can be among the things made for lending and renting, but if he does not usually lend it, it is not included, even though it is suitable for lending and renting.

For Rava took out etc.. Rava took these vessels from the orphans who held them, even though these things were not originally made for lending and renting, because there were witnesses that the owners were accustomed to lending and renting them (see Bavli Bava Metzia 116a, Shevuot 46b).
A pair of shears used for the sarbal. Large scissors used to cut coarse hides and hard things (Dictionary of Rabbi Tanchum Yerushalmi, entry "sarbal").

It follows that other shears and other scissors are not included in this law etc.. From this case one may infer that things regarding which no testimony was given that the owner is accustomed to lend or rent them are not among the vessels made for lending and renting, even though they are suitable for lending and renting.
To place it before his eyes and not let it depart. That he should remember it always and it should not leave his memory (based on Proverbs 3:21).

Both vessels made for lending and renting and other vessels. Unlike other people who have a presumption of ownership over movable property in their possession, except for things made for lending and renting (as above 8:3), a craftsman has no presumption over all the vessels he works with, since people are accustomed to give them to him for repair.
Since he could say, "I returned it to you". And since he could claim that he returned it, he is also believed when he claims that he sold it or gave it to him ("migo").
For one who deposits with his fellow before witnesses need not be repaid before witnesses. Therefore he could have claimed that he returned it to him.
And they do not require him to bring out the vessel. In order to show it, for they do not require him to impair his ability to make his claim.
As we have explained. Above, halachah 1.
You fixed. You set a fee.
If the vessel was visible before them. And it is also known that it belonged to the householder.

As we have explained in Sechirut. Hilchot Sechirut 11:8 (and there the Rambam wrote that the householder swears a heset oath; see Maggid Mishneh and Mirkevet HaMishneh there, who addressed this contradiction).
And he gives. He pays him only one for his wage.
He can claim up to its value. He can claim that he is owed wages up to the value of the item held in his hand.
As we have explained. Above 1:2.
A craftsman who gave up his craft. Who stopped practicing his trade.
As we have explained. Above 8:1.
In the presence of the householder. But if he entered not in the householder's presence, he must return in every case (see Hilchot Gezelah 4:12).
Its corners. The corners of his garment.

"Return to me the vessel I lent you," and here are the witnesses, and he says "It was bought by me" - he is not believed. But if the claimant claimed that he stole it from him, the defendant is believed to claim that he bought it from him, unless he is established as a thief (Hilchot Genevah 5:12).
For he is not accustomed to sell his vessels. He is not accustomed to sell his belongings.
Because he stored them away only in order to deny them. By default he put them away so that he could claim he did not take them out.
He swears a heset oath. The defendant.
Perhaps he needed money and sold. It is possible that the claimant needed money and sold them to the defendant.
As we have explained. Above 8:3.
And he has witnesses that this vessel... is known to him. The witnesses testify that they know the vessel is his.
Like land. That they are given to the one known as the owner, and not to the present holder, as below 11:1.

For since his father could not claim that he bought it or that it is a pledge. For these are vessels made for lending and renting, and therefore his claim that he bought them or that they are a pledge is not accepted.

So too this one cannot make him swear. If the heir does not know with certainty that his father bought the vessel, he cannot make the claimant swear. And the rule that the court makes claims for an heir that his father could have made does not help here, because this rule was not stated regarding a claim that can only obligate an oath, but regarding a claim that helps the claimant keep the item.
And we have already explained that there are those who ruled that the householder swears a heset oath. Even if the heir does not make a definite claim (above 8:3).
Axe. A hatchet.
For a person does not brazenly cut down a tree that is not his. And by default he acted lawfully.
Once it has been cut, it is like other movable property. That it is not taken from the one in whose possession it is (as above 8:1).

Even though the land is in the presumption of its owners etc.. Although regarding the land he is not believed to claim it is his by purchase, since he has no document, regarding the produce he is believed to claim he bought it, since no document is written for that.

And needless to say etc.. If he held the land for at least three years, he is certainly believed regarding the produce, since he could claim that he bought the entire land and the document is not now in his hand (see below 11:2-4).
Two who were holding one vessel. At its edge (see below, halachah 9).
And one leading. Walking on foot and leading the animal.
In an alley or a courtyard belonging to both of them. Which are places where both can acquire the item by the kinyan of pulling (see Hilchot Mechirah 4:3-5), and so both hold it equally.
He swears while taking an object that he has no less than half in this thing. And he does not swear that he has half in it, since that would contradict his claim to the whole.
And this oath is an enactment of the Sages etc.. By strict law they could have divided without an oath, since both hold it equally.
And this one takes three parts and this one takes a quarter. Since one half is agreed upon and the claims concern the other half, they divide that half between them.
If two were gripping a cloak. If each one holds a part of the body of the cloak and not only its edges.
After they swear. On half of what remains.
And each may roll over onto his fellow that everything he took he took lawfully. Each may demand of the other that he include in his oath that he also took lawfully what he held in his hand.
They divide all of it equally. Since they are not holding the body of the cloak.
And any division stated here is by value etc.. If dividing would damage the item, it is not divided into parts but its monetary value is divided.
It is in the presumption of the one holding all of it. And the other's grip does not count.
Since he was silent at first, it is as if he admitted to him. As if he admitted to him that the cloak is his, and since now the first holds the cloak, it cannot be taken from him without proof.

Even though the first cries out from beginning to end, they divide. For the silence of the second at first is not a definite admission that the cloak is the first's, but because of the doubt, the cloak is not taken from the first, who holds it. But after the second returned and snatched the cloak from the first, the law returned to its original state, that both parties hold the cloak equally, and therefore they divide.
He admitted to me. That it is mine.
I rented it to him. I rented him my share.

The one who takes from his fellow bears the burden of proof etc.. For movable property is judged according to the one who holds it, and a heset oath is sworn by the one who is claimed against (as above 8:1).
Known to its owners. Known to belong to another person.
For its being in his hand is not proof. Unlike other movable property, which is in the presumption of the one in whose hand it is (above 8:1).
Guarded or entrusted to a shepherd. That the owners or the shepherd do not let it go by itself.
It is in the presumption of the one in whose hand it is. Since it does not go freely, its law is that of any movable property.
He can claim up to its value etc.. As above 8:2.
This defendant brought... witnesses that this slave has been with him for three consecutive years. That the slave was with him for three years.
He is believed. Like the law of land, which is in the presumption of one who holds it for three years (below 11:2, 12:1).
Rather, it is mine as if I had inherited him. The force of my ownership is like ownership by inheritance.
As we have already explained. Above 7:8.
That a claimant may return and claim a matter that is implied. The defendant may return and make a new claim if it can be implied from the first claim he made.
A ship and the like etc.. Neither holds it in practice and neither has proof that it is his, and one asks the court not to let his fellow take control of it until he brings witnesses.
We do not seize. Initially the court does not intervene in the matter, and whoever prevails and seizes it acquires it (as below 15:4).
Or they may divide it willingly and with an oath, as we have explained. Above 9:7.
Those known to their owners. That have owners recognized as their owners.
And rents it. Leases it out.
That he ate the produce of this land for three consecutive years and benefited from all of it as everyone benefits from such land. See below, chapter 12.
For the people are busy in their markets. That everyone comes to the fairs held there.
Why were you not careful with your document?. For a buyer and a recipient usually have a document.
When I heard, I said, "Perhaps he merely insulted me". For he did not say that he would sue him in court.
And they write even though he did not say to them "write". For this is a benefit to the protester that they write his protest, and he loses nothing by it (compare above 7:2).
It is nothing. This is not a protest, and the holder of the land is believed to claim that he bought it.

The field stays in Reuven's hand, even if he claimed that Shimon sold it to him or gave it to him today. Although he has no three-year presumption, and even if he claimed he bought the field that very day.
And for the produce I brought him down, and the produce was his. That he sold him the produce only.
As we have explained. Above, halachah 2.
For they always yield fruit. Since benefit can be derived from them at any time.
And the cisterns, trenches, and caves. Which serve as water sources.
And the dovecotes. Cotes for pigeons.
And the olive presses. A compound for producing oil.
And an irrigated field that is watered constantly etc.. These do not rely only on rainwater and require daily tending (and so too with gardens and orchards).
As we have explained. Above 10:4.
And a tree field. Of large trees that need no irrigation and are not tended daily.
Once he has eaten three crops of one kind, they count as three years. But if he ate three crops not of one kind, it is not a presumptive ownership.
And he harvested. The picking of dates is called "gedirah."
Closely packed. Very close together.
For in the end they will dry up. Because of the density.
And he ate them for three years. Three crops that count as three years.
We rented from him. The holder rented the courtyard to us.
These witnesses who rented must bring proof that they lived in it continuously. And they cannot themselves serve as witnesses to the presumptive ownership by day and by night.

For this matter depends on them and does not depend on the holder's claim, so that they could testify for him. They cannot testify because the presumption rests on their dwelling in the courtyard. Since the subject of their testimony is their dwelling in the courtyard, which obligates them to pay rent to the true owners, they are also a party to the matter, and a litigant cannot testify (Even HaEzel; see Lechem Mishneh, Ohr Sameach and Even Yisrael).
The itinerants. Those who travel around the towns to trade and do not necessarily return to their homes every day.
We make the claim for him at the outset. We make the claim on behalf of the protester, even if he did not claim it himself.
And left it fallow. He did not sow it.
Even if he did so for several years. In a way that he sowed the field at least three years, but not consecutively.
Even though some of them sow year after year etc.. Even if it is not everyone's practice to leave fallow but only some of them, and he left it fallow, this is a presumptive ownership.
He ate it. He benefited from the field's yield.
For a document has publicity. And since the owner of the field knew that the two were working the field in partnership, he should have protested.

If they sold to one another by document, the three combine and this is a presumptive ownership. Since all of them held the land by virtue of the first holder, it is considered as if he held the land for three years. And since the sale was by document, it has publicity, and the protester cannot claim that he did not protest because he thought these were three separate people.

The father ate it one year and the son two etc.. The father died and the son inherited his father and continued to hold the field. Since the son eats by virtue of the father, they are considered one person for the purpose of presumptive ownership.
And that is so if he bought by document. As above, halachah 6.

And in the presence of his son two. After the father's death (and the case is where the son is an adult, since one cannot establish presumptive ownership over the property of a minor, as below 13:2, 14:7-9 - Maggid Mishneh; but above, halachah 7, the law applies even if the son is a minor - see Maggid Mishneh there).

Provided that the son sold this field among his fields. That the son did not sell the field explicitly and separately, but among the other fields he sold, and the holder can claim that he did not know this field was sold.
There is no greater protest than this. For the sale itself proves that the seller claims the field is his.
He plowed it. He plowed and did not sow.
Since he did not benefit from it etc.. Even though he tended it in the usual way, for presumptive ownership helps only if he ate fruit.
He opened its water channels. He opened the water channels that irrigate the field.

And he plowed and harrowed it. He performed agricultural work that prepares the soil for sowing (some explain that "pittuach" is the plowing before sowing and "shidud" is breaking up the clods - see Isaiah 28:24 and the commentators there).
He sowed a kor and gathered a kor. The amount of seed he collected equaled the amount he sowed.
He ate it as fodder. He cut and gathered the crop while it was still tender grass, fit only as animal feed.
He did not establish presumptive ownership. Since he benefited from the field only partially.
Orlah. Fruit that grows in the first three years after a tree is planted and is forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 10:6).
Sheviit. Fruit sown or planted in the Sabbatical year in violation of the prohibition, or that grew permissibly but may not be gathered all at once (Hilchot Shemittah 1:12, 4:1).
And kilayim. Fruit and crops that grew in violation of the prohibition of mixed kinds in a vineyard and are forbidden for benefit (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 10:9).
Flint. Hard rock.
On which to spread the fruit. To dry.
He was keeping an animal in a certain place in his fellow's courtyard etc.. If the courtyard belongs to partners, the law is different, as explained in Hilchot Shecheinim 5:5.
Outside the fence. In a place belonging to the protester, but whatever grows there is ownerless.
He did not establish presumptive ownership. In the area outside the fence.
From a beit rova. An area fit for sowing a quarter-kav.
Since etc.. As above, halachah 13.

As much as the space for his basket and his picking pole around every tree. One who holds trees gets around each tree the area needed for the picker to walk around the tree's branches along with the basket he carries.
And its ground. The area beneath it.
He has ground the thickness of the tree. The thickness of the trunk.
Within a beit shalosh se'in. Within an area of three beit se'ah (in total an area of fifty cubits by one hundred fifty cubits).
And the other trees did not bear fruit. So it turns out that each year he ate all the fruit that the trees in that field produced.

Where he ate some of the fruit and the people plundered the rest of the fruit. The fruit of the other trees, which he did not eat, was eaten by anyone who wished. Therefore in this case he has presumptive ownership only in the trees whose fruit he ate.
But if he left their fruit on them. And no one ate that fruit.
And these, the land is not left in their hands etc.. Their laws are detailed in this chapter and the next.
Even though they ate it for three years. And they also have a claim.
And sharecroppers. Those who work the field for a share of the produce.
And guardians. Those appointed to manage the money and property of others.
They are not particular with one another. The owners are not particular if these use their property.
As we have explained. Above 11:1.
Heads of the exile communities. Leaders of the public in the Diaspora.
Strongmen. Those who take others' money by force.
Because they have no claim etc.. Their claim does not count (see above 5:9), and presumptive ownership without a claim is of no help (below 14:12).
And likewise one who holds their property etc.. Since they do not protest against the holder (see below 14:7-9).
And the same law applies to the rest of them. To the others listed in the previous halachot.
They gave up their craft. They stopped practicing this craft.

For since he is a sharecropper of ancestral households. That he has worked for this family for years, and he is considered a sort of guardian of the owners' property (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 3:3).
But if this one was made a sharecropper originally. If he began as a sharecropper only with the present owner of the field.
And he ate all of it for the years of presumptive ownership. He ate all the fruit of the field and did not bring the owners any share of the crop.
And we say to the owners. The court argues against the owners.
How did he eat everything year after year and you did not protest?. Though a sharecropper has only part of the produce.
That he brought down sharecroppers under his hand. That he appointed sub-sharecroppers to work the land under his supervision.

But if he apportioned to other sharecroppers who were in it. That these sharecroppers were in the householder's fields previously too, but this sharecropper allots to each of them the field in which he will work.
Whether regarding other property. Of the protester, and not the field they held.
Whether the court appointed them. To be in charge of orphans' property.
Whether the orphans' father appointed them. While he was alive.

And the orphans grew up and left them. Left them in their position (but while the orphans are minors, in any case one cannot establish presumptive ownership over their property, since there is no presumptive ownership over a minor's property, as above, halachah 2).
Whether a person appointed guardians over his expenses and income. To manage his financial affairs.
And it is not subject to the law of division. It does not have enough area to be divided into two fields of reasonable size (see Hilchot Shecheinim 1:4).
It is in the presumption of both of them. Since the property cannot be divided, perhaps they agreed between them that each would work all of it for an extended period.

Even though he stipulated with her that he has no usufruct in her property. Basically a husband is entitled to eat the fruit of his wife's property, but they can stipulate in advance to cancel this right (see Hilchot Ishut 23:1-4).

And even if he stipulated with her when she was betrothed that he would not inherit her. That he also waived his right to inherit her (and this condition is effective only before the marriage - see there, halachot 5-6, Lechem Mishneh).
And afterward he ate, built, demolished, and did whatever he did. That he used the field as if it were his.
That he set aside a field for her sustenance and she ate other fields. He designated a particular field from whose fruit she would be sustained, and she eats the fruit of another field.
Their eating is not proof. For it is their way to be lenient with one another and to allow each to use the other's property.
Even if there is doubt about the divorce. Although she is not entirely considered divorced, nevertheless by default he is careful that she not eat the fruit of his fields.
Or those established as killing people over monetary matters. Even if they were not established as robbers regarding this field.
All these whose eating is not proof. Those mentioned in the previous chapter.
And a husband in his wife's property. For she can claim that she sold to him for the sake of marital peace and did not really want to sell.
In what property did they say this?. That a husband has no proof in his wife's property.

In iron-sheep property. Property that the woman brought with her at the time of marriage, for which the husband took responsibility to return its value in the event of divorce or widowhood (Hilchot Ishut 16:1).
In a field set aside for her in her ketubah. From which she will collect her ketubah.
And in a field he wrote for her in her ketubah. As an addition to the ketubah.
And in a field he gave her from his own. That he gave her a special field to add to the dowry in addition to the property she brought from her father's house (see there 23:11).

But in usufruct property he has proof. For usufruct property belongs entirely to the wife and the husband is only entitled to eat its fruit; therefore she is not afraid to refuse if her husband wants her to confirm in a document that she sold or gave it to him.
As we have explained in Hilchot Ishut. 22:15-18.
Since he was established as a robber regarding this field. That it is known that he robbed the field, but he claims that he afterward bought it from the owner lawfully.
Out of fear. Fear of the robber.
And he has nothing. The robber does not receive the field's price from the owners even if he claims he paid for it.
He counted out such and such for him. He gave the owner a certain sum for the field.
