As we have explained in Hilchot Gezelah. 9:14-16: since he was established as a robber, the seller's claim is accepted and the sale is void from the outset.
They have presumptive ownership. Like anyone.
And if they claimed that it is an inheritance from their fathers... they have no presumptive ownership. Since their fathers could not have made a claim to the field.
As we have explained. Above, halachah 2.
Even if he comes on his father's claim. And not on his own claim.
He comes on the claim of his father's father. The robber.
His eating is not proof. As above 13:2.
And an Israelite who comes by virtue of a gentile. He holds the field and claims he bought or received it from the gentile, while the protester claims it is his and he did not sell it to the gentile.
There is no presumptive ownership over a minor's property. Since he cannot protest against the holder.
Even if he came of age. Even if the years of holding were completed after he came of age.
One who held a minor's property for many years. Held the orphan's land after the father died, and it was not known that it was his father's.
They are a pledge in my hand, and I have a debt on them of such and such. They are with me as a pledge for a debt that the land's owner owes me.
And he collects from its rent what he claimed, and it returns to the orphans. He collects his debt from the land's produce and then returns it to the orphans.
And the field and all the fruit he ate return to the orphans. Since it became clear that he ate the fruit unlawfully.
He ate it for the years of presumptive ownership during their father's lifetime. For this is a valid presumptive ownership.

And he collects it without an oath, since he could have said "it is mine". And he does not swear a heset oath, since the orphans do not make a definite claim against him, and one does not swear a heset oath on a claim of doubt, as above 1:7 (Maggid Mishneh).
Because he is occupied with himself. And is too preoccupied to protest.
One who flees because of money. So that money will not be taken from him.
In the property of a married woman. Property in which her husband also has a right.
"You sold to me, and your husband". With the consent of both of you.
Until this protester brings witnesses that it is his. And the protest alone is not enough.
And we do not open for this holder at first. We do not ask him whether he has a claim of ownership.
And the document is found void. For example, it is invalid.
The presumptive ownership is nullified. Since his claim is based on the document in his hand and the document was found invalid.
One who comes by virtue of inheritance. Who claims he inherited the property.
By virtue of his father. On the basis of his father's ownership.
And this land was not known to be his forefathers'. It was not established that the land belonged to those he inherits from.
He brought proof that his father was seen in it. That he was seen in the field.
To inspect it. To examine it for purchase.

Since he admitted to him that it is his and that he did not take it from him. And although he claims he bought the land from another, since there is no knowledge that the seller had ownership of the land, the buyer's claim is baseless.

We say to him at first, "Validate your document". The court tells him to authenticate the witnesses' signatures on the deed of sale, and does not rely only on the presumptive ownership (for the method of validating a document see Hilchot Edut 6:2).
And he will be judged by the document. He will be judged on the basis of the document and will win the land even without having proved his presumptive ownership.

And if it is impossible for him to validate it. For example, the witnesses are not available and no one recognizes their signatures (but if it turns out that the document is invalid, we do not rely on the presumptive ownership - see above 14:12).
That he ate it as wheat. The field's yield was wheat.
One testified that this one ate it the first, third, and fifth year etc.. In a place where they sow in alternate years, and likewise hold, as above 12:4 (Maggid Mishneh).
For in the year this one testifies about, the other did not testify about it. And for each year there is only partial testimony (see also Hilchot Edut 4:7).
And the land and the fruit return. The holder must return to the owners the land and the fruit he ate unlawfully.
Who is closer to him and fit to inherit. Who is closer to the deceased in the order of precedence in the laws of inheritance (see Hilchot Nachalot, chapter 1).
They leave it between them. Without a ruling by the court.
And whoever overpowers shall go down into it. Shall take hold of the field (for a similar law see above 10:6).
And the one. The one who did not prevail and take hold of it.
And if a third came. While they are disputing over the field, a third person came who has no claim or proof equal to theirs.

And they leave it in the hand of the one for whom the witnesses of presumptive ownership testified that it was his fathers'. Although their testimony about the presumptive ownership was contradicted, we accept the rest of their testimony that it belonged to his forefathers and decide on that basis.
For this testimony too is found contradicted. It turns out that the testimony about the first's ancestral ownership is also void and neither has proof.
And this one brought witnesses that he ate it for the years of presumptive ownership. And he claims it by virtue of his presumptive ownership.
For he did not claim anything against him. The first did not make a claim against the testimony that it belonged to the second's forefathers, for he did not explain how it came into his hands.
For every presumptive ownership etc.. As above 14:12.
He relies on it. He is confident that it is mine.
For he gave a reason for his first words. He explained his intention in his first claim.
"My fathers', not your fathers'". And it is implied from his words that he completely denies the other's words.

We do not listen to him in this other claim. After the protester brought witnesses against the holder's first claim, the holder cannot return and make a new claim unless he explains how the first claim could be interpreted in accordance with what he now claims. In the case at hand his new claim contradicts the first, and therefore it is not accepted (see above 7:8).
I took it from Levi four years ago. Four years ago, and I bought it before you.

For a person calls many years "years of presumptive ownership". Therefore when Reuven said "I bought this field from Levi and ate it for the years of presumptive ownership," it can be interpreted that he meant he bought it many years ago and not specifically three years ago.

For there is no greater protest by Levi than this, since he sold it before Reuven established presumptive ownership. Since Levi sold the field to Shimon before Reuven held the field for three years, the sale itself counts as a protest against Reuven who held the field, and since he did not hold the field three years without protest, it is taken from him.
This one says, "It is my fathers'," and brought witnesses. That it was his forefathers'.
And this one says, "It is my fathers'," and has no witnesses. And he claims that he held the field for the years of presumptive ownership and ate its fruit.
For he says that he ate by virtue of his fathers. And he admitted eating the fruit.
A validated document. A document that was confirmed and authenticated in court.
He is believed. To claim that he bought the field by another document that was lost.
Even one day. Within the period in which he claims he bought it from him.
And he lost the way to his field. He does not know where the path is in his fellow's field, through which he had been established to pass to his own field.
The four bought from one. The fields were owned by one person, and four people bought parts of his field.
For a hundred maneh. Or any sum that may be required to pay.
Or fly in the air. That is, he cannot compel any of them to give him a path in his field, since he has no proof that his path once passed in this place.
He has no path through him. He cannot demand that he give him a path, even though it is clear that he had a path in one of the fields they bought.
You cannot pass over any one of them. For each of the four could reject him.
And he was the owner of its boundary from beginning to end. He was the owner of the fields bordering the other's field the whole time.
And let him go by whichever the owner of the fields wishes. The owner of the surrounding fields gives him whichever path he wishes.

And if he established a path and said "this is my path". If the field owner took a certain path and established it, he is now in possession of the path, so if the owner of the surrounding fields wants to remove him and give him another path, he must bring proof (Kesef Mishneh; see Piskei VeShittot).
One of the witnesses of the document. The deed of sale.
We do not listen to him and we do not pay attention to proofs he brings about that field. His claim is no claim, even if he brings proofs for his claim.
How can you testify to the sale and then turn around and protest?. For his testimony is like an admission and confirmation that the field is Reuven's.

And likewise if Levi testified in a document etc.. Even if he did not testify to the sale of the field he is protesting, but to the sale of another field, and the document states that it is next to Reuven's field, he cannot protest against the field that is stated to belong to Reuven.

The witness claimed and said etc.. If the witness claims that his testimony refers only to the furrow adjacent to the border of the field sold, his claim is accepted and he can protest regarding the rest of the field.
But the judge who validated the document. If he was one of the judges who confirmed the signatures on the document (see Hilchot Edut 6:1).

Because the judges may validate the document even though they did not read it. For the role of the validating judges is only to authenticate the witnesses' signatures, and they do not deal with the document's content (there, halachah 8).
But the witnesses do not sign a document unless they have read all of it etc.. See Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 24:5.
I am buying. I intend to buy.
On your advice that we buy it. Do you advise me to buy it?
Levi may protest against it. And claim that it was not the seller's but his.
For he did not perform an act. He did not testify to the sale or the like, but only gave advice.
For yesterday. Yesterday, and this is an admission that the field is mine and was not the seller's from whom you bought.
This is not proof. For he did not perform an act, and therefore he can explain his words (and as above, halachah 3).
Even though I do not know whether it is yours or not. And since the protester has no proof that it is his, the field is left in the holder's hand.
That this field is his. That it is held as his.
"You ate it by robbery". You ate from it after you robbed it.

Whether or not there were witnesses there that he ate etc.. In any case where the land is taken from the holder, he does not have to pay for its fruit, since we know he ate the fruit only from his own words, and if we rely on his words that he ate it for three years, he has presumptive ownership along with his claim.

He is liable to an oath but cannot swear, and pays. For the protester claims fruit on the basis of the witness, and the holder cannot swear, since he does not contradict the witness but claims that he ate lawfully (see above 4:8).
If they were not known. It is not clear what he ate or how much he ate.
A definite claim. A definite claim of how much he ate.
And they place a ban on whoever ate more and does not pay. For an explanation of the ban see above 1:4 in the commentary.
Anyone who returns land from under his hand. And is obligated to return its fruit as well.
He leased it. He rented it out.
They collect the rent from them a second time etc.. Since they did not pay the true owner of the field.
A person is forbidden to make false claims. Even if he does not intend to keep money that is not his.

He shall not claim two hundred from him in order that he admit to a maneh and become liable to an oath. In order to obligate him to a severe oath while holding a sacred object (since in any case he can make him swear a heset oath); thus he perverts the law by obligating him to an oath that he is not liable for (Yad Peshutah).
He owed him a maneh and he claimed two hundred. The claimant lied and claimed two hundred from him, and the defendant truly owed a hundred.

He shall not say, "I will deny everything in court and admit to him a maneh privately". Since he wants to delay payment of the maneh to another time (for to be exempt from the oath of partial admission he could have brought him the maneh he admits to now and been exempt by the law of "here, take it"); so it turns out that he lies to delay the judgment (there).
There were three, each owed a maneh by one person. Three people, to each of whom the defendant owes a maneh.
And he denied them. Before they came to court.
One shall not claim. He shall not claim for himself the three manehs that the defendant owes to the three.
And two testify. And the other two testify as he says, so that they can collect the entire debt from the defendant, even though in this way they prevent him from evading payment of the debt.
Keep far from a false matter. One must keep far from speaking false words even if they are meant to collect money that is due by law.
